title: Why Buildings Stand Up
objective: After this level you can explain how weight flows down through a building to the ground.
summary: Buildings carry dead loads (themselves) and live loads (people, weather). Every load follows a load path to the soil, and each part is squeezed (compression) or stretched (tension).

cards.headline: Every building is carrying something heavy: itself.
cards.body: Before anyone walks in, a building is already holding up its own floors, walls and roof. Standing up means getting all of that weight, plus yours, safely down into the ground. Here's how.

cards.headline: Dead loads and live loads
cards.body: Engineers sort weight into two kinds. Dead loads are permanent: the structure's own weight plus its roofing, flooring, pipes and inside walls. Live loads come and go: people, sofas, pianos, books, cars. Weather counts as a live load too, and wind pushes sideways rather than down. A floor has to be ready for both, including the day your friend moves in with a piano.

cards.headline: Follow the weight down
cards.body: Every load needs a route to the ground, and engineers call that route the load path. A continuous path runs from the roof, through the walls, to the foundation, and finally into the soil that holds the building up. Here's an analogy: a stack of books on a table. The bottom book carries every book above it, and the table carries the lot. Take one link out and the weight has nowhere to go.

mascot.line: Next time you stand on a floor, you are part of a load path. Welcome aboard.

cards.fact: Every piece of that path is being squeezed or stretched.
cards.context: Engineers name two basic forces. Compression pushes and squeezes; tension pulls and stretches. A post carrying weight down to the ground is squeezed. A cable holding up a hanging load is stretched. Keep both words handy: the rest of this chapter is about which parts get squeezed, which get stretched, and which materials can take it.

cards.headline: Standing up: explained
learned: Dead loads are permanent; live loads come and go
Every load follows a load path down to the soil
Posts are squeezed; hanging cables are stretched

questions.prompt: Which of these is a live load on a building's floor?

options.label: The weight of the floor itself
options.rationale: That's permanent, so it's a dead load.

options.label: The pipes and ducts
options.rationale: Fixed pipes and ducts count as dead load.

options.label: The inside partition walls
options.rationale: Partition walls are permanent: dead load.

questions.explanation: Live loads come and go, like people, furniture and pianos; the structure and its fixed parts are dead load.

questions.prompt: Why does a building need a continuous load path?

options.label: So heat can rise from the basement to the roof
options.rationale: A load path carries forces, not heat.

options.label: So people can find a way out in a fire
options.rationale: That's an escape route, not a load path.

options.label: So every load can reach the soil beneath it
So the walls never have to carry anything
options.rationale: Walls are often part of the path.

questions.explanation: A continuous load path carries loads from the roof, through the walls and foundation, into the supporting soil.

questions.prompt: In a stack of books on a table, the bottom book carries all the others. Which force is it under?

options.label: Tension, because it is stretched
options.rationale: Nothing is pulling on it; it's being pressed.

options.label: No force, because the table holds it
options.rationale: The table holds it up, but the books above still press down on it.

options.label: Only sideways wind force
options.rationale: The weight above presses straight down.

questions.explanation: Like a post carrying weight to the ground, the bottom book is pressed from above and below: compression.
